title: Clinic and hospital equipment: batteries, pumps, motors, heaters, lights and tubing
summary: Clinic and hospital equipment is a good source of lithium and lead-acid batteries, stepper motors and lead screws from syringe pumps, vacuum pumps from suction units, autoclave heaters, solenoid valves, exam lights, actuators and clean tubing. Allow about 40 minutes a unit. Decide first whether someone still needs it; the main dangers are blood and needles, mains power and lithium packs.

steps.text: Decide whether to take it apart at all. Working equipment is worth more working: a suction unit, an autoclave, an exam table, a monitor or an infusion pump can help a clinic or a carer today. Leave it where it is, or carry it whole to someone who can use it. Strip only what is broken, abandoned or no longer useful.

Protect yourself: thick gloves over nitrile gloves, glasses, a mask, boots with stiff soles. Assume every surface, tube, bin and drawer is contaminated. Don't reach blindly into drawers or bins, and don't open sharps boxes. Pick up loose needles with pliers and drop them point-first into a hard bottle with a lid.
steps.warn: Used needles and blood carry hepatitis, HIV and tetanus. Wash with soap and running water after any needle prick or contact and get help (see biohazard).

steps.text: Know what to leave: defibrillators and any imaging equipment (X-ray, CT, MRI), anything with a radiation, laser or UV warning label, mercury blood-pressure gauges and thermometers, gas cylinders (oxygen cylinders too; see compressed_gas), and anything leaking a chemical.
steps.warn: X-ray, defibrillator and imaging machines hold lethal voltage or radiation. Don't open them.

steps.text: Unplug it and wait at least 10 minutes. Wipe the outside with soap and water, then with 1 part bleach to 10 parts water, and leave it wet for 5 minutes. Open the case with security bits if needed. Check for large capacitors beside the power supply and discharge them before you touch any board (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: Power supplies in medical units can hold a charge for days. Measure before you touch.

steps.text: Take the batteries first. Lithium-ion packs sit behind battery doors on monitors and pumps; sealed lead-acid batteries (12 V, 2-7 Ah) sit in the base of older monitors, suction units and carts. Take them out, tape the contacts and look at them: swollen, hot or leaking ones go outdoors (see safety_swollen_lithium and safety_lead_acid). Test the good ones as in test_lithium_cell and test_lead_acid.
steps.warn: A short across a lithium pack or a lead-acid battery can start a fire. Tape the contacts at once.

steps.text: Infusion and syringe pumps: open the case, undo the stepper motor with its lead screw or the peristaltic roller assembly, and lift out the pressure sensor and the display. Take clean parts only, and wash with soap and water if there is any residue.
Suction units: take the small diaphragm vacuum pump with its motor (12 V or mains). Leave the collection jar, its lid and its tubing behind: they hold infectious fluid. Don't blow through the pump.
steps.warn: Pump heads and tubing may hold infected fluid. Wear gloves and wash your hands afterwards.

steps.text: Autoclaves and steam steriliser: let it cool for hours, open the vent and drain the water. Open the door only when the pressure gauge reads zero. Take out the heating element (1-2 kW, usually bolted under the chamber), the solenoid valves and the pressure and temperature switches. Leave the pressure chamber whole.
steps.warn: Steam and hot water scald badly. Never open a pressure vessel under pressure, and never cut, drill or weld the chamber.

steps.text: Lights and tables: unplug exam lights, support the arm, then unbolt the lamp head. Power exam tables and dental chairs have electric actuators under the seat or table: block the table or chair level, then undo the actuator's pins. If the cylinder is oil-filled (hydraulic), leave it.
steps.warn: Spring-balanced light arms can fly up when the lamp head comes off, and a table or chair can drop when its actuator is removed. Support them first.

steps.text: Tubing, probes and screens: take only unopened sealed tubing and clean probes (pulse oximeter and temperature probes). Leave anything that has been inside a patient. Take LCD screens from monitors; don't pry at them.
Label what you took and store it dry. Wash your hands and tools with soap and water, then check batteries again in a day.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Batteries.** Medical packs are usually good-quality cells in a case with a gauge board. 12 V 2-7 Ah sealed lead-acid batteries power lights, alarms and radios. Many Li-ion packs are 10-15 V (3-4 cells); the cells inside are standard 18650 types (see build_18650_pack).
- **Stepper motors with lead screws.** Quiet, precise linear motion: a camera slider, a micro-dosing pump, a small CNC axis.
- **Diaphragm vacuum pump.** Moves air or gives vacuum from 12 V: aquarium air, degassing, small filters, suction for drains.
- **Heating elements.** 1-2 kW autoclave heaters: a water heater, a still, a drying oven. Wire them to mains safely and fuse them.
- **Solenoid valves.** For water, air and gas switching in builds.
- **Exam lights.** LED lights run on 12-24 V: work lights for a shelter or a workshop.
- **Actuators.** The 24 V linear actuators lift a bed, a hatch or a tracker.
- **Silicone and PVC tubing.** Good for siphons, filters, pumps and drip feeds. Sealed sterile spares can also go back to a clinic.
- **Probes.** Pulse oximeter probes (LEDs and a light sensor) and thermistor probes can be reused as sensors.

## Safety and care

- Old LCD screens lit by fluorescent tubes hold a little mercury: don't break them.
- Disinfectants and sterilising chemicals (glutaraldehyde, alcohol, ethylene oxide cartridges) stay with their equipment. Keep them out of your eyes and away from heat.
- Wash everything you keep.

## What to leave

- X-ray, CT, MRI, radiation and laser equipment.
- Defibrillators.
- Oxygen cylinders and gas systems, unless you know them.
- Anything with fluid inside, contaminated waste and sharps.
